claims.text: In fully disordered multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys, Tc is primarily governed by local vibrational dynamics.
Constituent-element masses and bonding characteristics modulate the local vibrational dynamics.
Replacing lighter elements with heavier elements lowers the average phonon frequencies.
Lower phonon frequencies weaken electron-phonon coupling in the proposed alloy.
The weakened electron-phonon coupling caused by heavier-element substitution decreases Tc.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 is an example of a well-characterized, single-phase Nb-Ta-based high-entropy superconductor.
Nb-Ta-based disordered high-entropy alloys can exhibit bulk superconductivity described by weak-coupling BCS theory.
The proposed controlled intervention is to substitute lighter and heavier elements while preserving the single-phase, chemically disordered structure.
A high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements, each at a concentration of at least 5 at.%.
Controlled elemental substitution changes the phonon-frequency distribution through mass and bonding differences.
Shifts in the local vibrational spectrum modify electron-phonon coupling strength.
Substitution of heavier elements weakens coupling, whereas reverse substitution could strengthen coupling and raise Tc.
Tc will decrease systematically relative to the baseline when substitution reduces average phonon frequencies.
The magnitude of the Tc shift will correlate with the measured change in the local vibrational spectrum if other superconducting parameters remain similar.
The unmodified Nb-Ta-based baseline exhibits robust zero-resistance superconductivity.
The baseline superconductivity is BCS-like and electron-phonon mediated.

The hypothesis is restricted to chemically disordered, single-phase HEAs whose superconductivity is predominantly electron-phonon mediated and is not dominated by magnetic impurities or strong correlations.
Electronic structure, including valence-electron-related changes, may influence Tc independently of the proposed vibrational effect.
The quantitative relationship between vibrational-spectrum changes and Tc shifts has not been established.
Failure of Tc to track the measured phonon-frequency shift under the controlled substitution would falsify the proposed vibrational-control hypothesis.
